title: Revives the dead (Berakhot 58b)
hookLine: seeing a friend after a year, one blesses the One who revives the dead
tomorrow: is there a blessing just for opening your eyes in the morning?
last: ALL THIS WAS DONE FOR ME.

cards: At an airport arrivals gate, somebody always screams. A year apart, and then a face comes around the corner, and nobody says anything sensible. So what do you say to a friend you haven't seen in a year?
The Talmud has the words. Blessed is the One who revives the dead. It sounds like too much, until you hear why.

teach.b: Here's the rule. See a friend after thirty days, and you bless God who has kept us alive and brought us to this time.
After twelve months, you say: who revives the dead. Rav explains the year.

The dead are forgotten from the heart only after twelve months, and he reads a psalm about being forgotten like the dead, out of mind. A year is long enough for someone to slip out of the everyday heart.
Seeing them again isn't only nice. It's a small return from the forgotten, so it gets the words that the Amidah uses for God who gives life.

teach.h: A WEEK OF BLESSING THE ORDINARY.
teach.b: Now look back at the week. Rava sent a man to bless the place of his rescue. The Mishnah said bless for the bad too, with both inclinations.
A dream was a letter unread. A sound, a sight and a smell restored a person.
A crowd held every mind different. And Ben Zoma found it all ready for him. Every one of these is the same move: notice the ordinary thing, and give it its blessing.

how: Jewish law gives a blessing on seeing a dear friend after thirty days (shehecheyanu) and after twelve months (mechayeh ha-metim, who revives the dead); the same phrase praises God in the Amidah.

o: a blessing for a doctor who saved someone's life
a prayer said only at a funeral or a grave
a blessing on seeing a friend after a year apart

s: 'who revives the dead' is only said at funerals
the Talmud gives it for seeing a friend after twelve months.
the Talmud gives one blessing for a friend after thirty days and another after a year
thirty days: who has kept us alive; twelve months: who revives the dead.

games.q: you run into a teammate who moved away two years ago. it's awkward; you never texted. your instinct is a quick "hey" and walk on. what does today's page suggest?
o: stop and greet them big: someone almost forgotten from the heart is back.
keep it quick; after this long, a big greeting would feel fake.
apologize first for not texting, then decide whether to talk.
games.why: after twelve months the Talmud blesses God who revives the dead. the return of someone nearly forgotten from the heart is worth that much.

practice: Bring to mind one friend you haven't seen in a long time. Let their face come back: the voice, the laugh, the way they stood. Notice how much of them was still there, waiting, and hold that for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Revives the dead: the Talmud's blessing for a friend seen after a year, someone almost forgotten from the heart, returned.

orig.note: Hebrew: who revives the dead; said on seeing a friend after twelve months.

carryVoice: For the next long-awaited hug: revives the dead, said with a laugh if you like. Thirty-nine down, eleven to go.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 58b (a friend after thirty days: shehecheyanu; after twelve months: who revives the dead; Rav: the dead are forgotten from the heart only after twelve months)
